title: I/O software and disk scheduling
subtitle: Devices are slow and strange. The OS hides that with layers — and orders disk requests to keep the head from wandering. This chapter covers device controllers, the three ways to move data, driver layering, disk arithmetic, the six scheduling algorithms, RAID and flash.

sections.title: Devices and their controllers
sections.body:
An I/O device has two parts. The device itself does the mechanical or electronic work — spin a platter, scan a key matrix, modulate a signal. The controller (or adapter) is the electronics that the computer talks to: a small chip with registers — a status register (“busy”, “error”, “data ready”), a command register, and a data buffer. The CPU controls the device by reading and writing those registers, either through special I/O instructions on a separate I/O address space (port-mapped I/O) or by ordinary loads and stores to addresses that are wired to the controller instead of RAM (memory-mapped I/O, the common approach today).

Devices differ enormously, which is the OS designer’s headache. By how data is moved they are block devices (disks, SSDs: data in fixed-size blocks, random access possible) or character devices (keyboards, serial ports: a stream of bytes, no seeking). By speed they span nine orders of magnitude, as the table shows. The OS’s job is to give them all one uniform interface — in Unix, “everything is a file”: open, read, write, close work on a disk file, a terminal and a network socket alike — while handling the differences below that line.

choices.text: Controller registers appear at ordinary memory addresses, so normal load/store instructions talk to the device.
Copying a device’s data into RAM with DMA.
Mapping a file into a process’s address space.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: No special I/O instructions are needed; protection can be done with the memory-management hardware.

sections.title: Three ways to move data: polling, interrupts, DMA
sections.body:
Suppose a program wants 4 KB from a device. In programmed I/O (polling) the CPU repeatedly reads the status register until it says “ready”, then copies one byte or word, and repeats for the whole block. It is simple and has no latency of its own, but the CPU does nothing else while the device works — hopeless for slow devices. In interrupt-driven I/O the CPU starts the operation and goes off to run another process; when the device is ready it raises an interrupt, a handler copies one unit of data, and the CPU returns to its work. Waiting costs nothing, but the CPU still copies every byte and takes one interrupt per unit — at high data rates the interrupts alone can saturate the processor.

Direct memory access (DMA) solves this for block devices. The driver tells a DMA controller the memory address, the byte count and the direction; the controller then moves the whole block between the device and RAM on its own, stealing bus cycles, and interrupts the CPU once at the end. For a 4 KB transfer interrupt-driven I/O might take thousands of interrupts, DMA takes one. The CPU only sets up and cleans up. The figure shows the sequence; the worked example puts numbers on the saving.

worked.why: A device delivers 100,000 bytes per second. Interrupt-driven I/O takes one interrupt per byte, each costing the CPU 5 µs. What fraction of the CPU is spent on interrupts?
Half the CPU. Now use DMA with 4,096-byte blocks and the same 5 µs per interrupt.
Time spent: 24.4 × 5 µs ≈ 122 µs per second.

problems.prompt: A disk transfers 8 MB/s in 512-byte blocks and each interrupt costs 10 µs of CPU. Compute the CPU load from interrupts with one interrupt per block (DMA), and with one interrupt per byte.
problems.answer: Per block: 8,000,000 / 512 = 15,625 interrupts/s × 10 µs = 0.156 s/s = 15.6 %. Per byte: 8,000,000 × 10 µs = 80 s per second — impossible: the CPU cannot keep up (8000 % load). DMA is essential.

sections.title: The I/O software stack
sections.body:
I/O software is organised in layers so that the ugly, device-specific parts are confined to the bottom. From the hardware upwards: interrupt handlers do the minimum urgent work and wake the driver; device drivers know one family of devices — its registers, its command set, its quirks — and translate generic requests (“read block 42”) into controller commands; the device-independent layer provides what all devices need — a uniform interface and naming (/dev/sda), buffering, caching, error reporting, protection and allocation of dedicated devices; and user-level libraries and spoolers sit on top.

Three services in the middle layer deserve their own names. Buffering keeps data in a memory area while it moves between a device and a process, smoothing speed mismatches and allowing one request to overlap the next (double buffering). Caching keeps recently used data in fast memory (the buffer cache holds disk blocks so repeated reads never reach the disk). Spooling queues output for a device that cannot be shared — a printer — so that many programs can “print” at once and a daemon feeds the printer one job at a time (which also removes the mutual-exclusion condition for deadlock). I/O calls may be blocking (the process sleeps until completion — simplest), non-blocking (returns immediately with whatever is available) or asynchronous (returns immediately and signals when finished, as in io_uring or Windows overlapped I/O).

problems.prompt: Distinguish buffering, caching and spooling in one line each.
problems.answer: Buffering: temporary holding of data in transit between producer and consumer of different speeds. Caching: keeping a copy of frequently used data in faster storage to avoid slower access. Spooling: queuing a job’s output on disk for a non-shareable device that processes it later.

sections.title: How a disk spends its time
sections.body:
A magnetic disk is a stack of spinning platters with one head per surface on a common arm. A track is a ring on one surface; the tracks at the same arm position on all surfaces form a cylinder; a track is divided into sectors, the smallest unit transferred (512 bytes historically, 4 KB now). Reading or writing a sector takes three phases. Seek time: move the arm to the right cylinder — typically 4–12 ms and by far the slowest part. Rotational latency: wait for the wanted sector to rotate under the head — on average half a revolution. Transfer time: read the sector as it passes — tiny for one sector. Access time = seek + latency + transfer.

The numbers explain two facts about disks. Random access is slow: each random 4 KB read costs about 13 ms, so a disk sustains roughly 75 random operations per second regardless of how fast its sequential transfer rate is. Sequential access is fast: after one seek and latency the head streams data at 100–200 MB/s. Hence every file system tries to keep a file’s blocks contiguous, and every scheduler tries to reduce arm movement. SSDs have no arm, so these algorithms matter for spinning disks only.

worked.why: A 7200 rpm disk turns once every 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms. On average the wanted sector is half a turn away.
Average seek time 9 ms. Transfer of one 4 KB block at 150 MB/s: 4096 / 150,000,000 s.
Random operations per second the disk can sustain:

sections.title: Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK
sections.body:
When several requests are queued, the order in which the arm visits cylinders decides the total head movement. Take head at 53 and requests 98 183 37 122 14 124 65 67 on a 200-cylinder disk. FCFS serves in arrival order — fair, but the arm zig-zags: 640 cylinders. SSTF (shortest seek time first) always picks the nearest request: 236, a big saving, but it behaves like SJF and can starve far requests when new nearby ones keep arriving.

The SCAN or elevator algorithm sweeps the arm from one end to the other, serving requests on the way, then reverses — like a lift in a building. No request waits more than two sweeps, so it cannot starve. Going up first costs 331; going down first costs 236. LOOK is SCAN that reverses at the last request in each direction instead of going to the disk edge: 299. The circular variants C-SCAN (382) and C-LOOK (322) serve in one direction only and jump back to the start after each sweep, which gives a more uniform waiting time (the cylinders at the edges are not visited twice per cycle).

Which to use? SSTF and LOOK are reasonable defaults; SCAN-style algorithms win when the load is heavy; FCFS is fine when requests are few. In practice the best choice also depends on the file-allocation method and on the controller, which reorders requests itself — modern disks with native command queuing do much of this internally.

worked.why: Head at 53, moving up. SSTF order: nearest first. Distances: 65 is 12 away, 67 is 14 away, 37 is 16 away — pick 65.
From 65 the nearest is 67 (2); from 67 the nearest is 37 (30)… Continue until all eight are served and add the moves.

sections.title: Disk management: formatting, boot blocks and swap
sections.body:
A fresh disk is just magnetic surface. Low-level formatting divides it into sectors, each with a header, a data area and an error-correcting code (ECC) trailer. The OS then writes its own structures: it partitions the disk into one or more logical disks, and creates a file system on each (logical formatting: an empty directory, free-space map, and so on). The first sector holds the boot block and partition table (the MBR we met in Chapter 1). Sectors that fail are recorded as bad blocks: simple controllers keep a list and skip them, smarter ones remap a bad sector to a spare sector kept in each cylinder (sector sparing) so the file system never sees it.

Disk space is also used for swap space — the backing store for virtual memory from the previous section. Swap can be a dedicated partition (no file-system overhead, fast) or a file. Because swap holds pages no longer than a process lives and is accessed in page-sized units, it is managed with simpler, faster allocation than ordinary files.

choices.text: The controller remaps a failed sector to a spare one so the file system does not see the defect.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Sparing reserves a few spare sectors, not half the disk.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is mirroring, not sparing.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It hides bad sectors below the file-system layer.

sections.title: RAID: reliability and speed from many disks
sections.body:
A single disk is slow compared with a CPU and fails sooner or later. RAID (redundant array of independent disks) combines several disks to gain speed, reliability or both, while looking like one disk to the OS. The two basic tools are striping (splitting data into blocks laid out round-robin over the disks, so several blocks can be read at once) and redundancy (extra copies or parity that allow reconstruction).

  • RAID 0 stripes only: n× the speed and capacity, but any single failure loses everything — reliability is worse than one disk.
  • RAID 1 mirrors: every block is written to two disks. It survives a failure and reads can be served from either, at the price of half the capacity.
  • RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity: for each stripe one block holds the XOR of the others, and the parity block rotates among the disks so no disk is a bottleneck. Any one lost block is recoverable by XOR-ing the survivors; usable capacity is (n − 1)/n. The weakness is the small-write penalty: updating one data block needs four I/Os (read old data, read old parity, write new data, write new parity).
  • RAID 6 keeps two independent parities and survives two simultaneous failures — important with very large disks, where a rebuild takes hours and a second failure during it is likely. RAID 10 (a stripe of mirrors) combines speed and safety at 50 % capacity.

worked.why: Three data blocks 1011, 0110, 1100. Parity is the bitwise XOR.
If the second disk dies, XOR the others with the parity: 1011 ⊕ 1100 ⊕ 0001 = 0110 — recovered.
Why does that work? XOR is its own inverse: A ⊕ B ⊕ C ⊕ (A ⊕ B ⊕ C) = 0, so any one term equals the XOR of all the others.

sections.title: Stable storage
sections.body: A single disk write can be interrupted by a crash, leaving a half-written block, and a disk can silently lose a block altogether. Stable storage is an abstraction that makes a write all-or-nothing: it either completes correctly or leaves the old value intact. It uses two copies of every block, ideally on different disks. To write: write the first copy and verify it by reading it back; only then write the second copy and verify it. After a crash, a recovery routine compares each pair. If both copies are good and equal, nothing to do. If one has a bad checksum, copy the good one over it. If both are good but different (the crash fell between the two writes), copy the first over the second. At most one copy is ever damaged by a single crash, so a valid value always survives. Databases build their transaction logs on this idea.

questions.prompt: Why are two copies written one after the other rather than together?

choices.text: So a crash can damage at most one of them.
Disks cannot write two blocks at once.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is slower; safety is the point.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sequential writes guarantee that one copy is always intact and verified.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Independent disks can; the ordering is deliberate.

problems.prompt: After a crash the recovery routine finds copy A good with value 17 and copy B good with value 12. What does it do, and what value does the system see?
problems.answer: Both copies are valid but different — the crash happened between the two writes. Recovery copies A over B, so the system sees 17 (the new value, whose write had completed on the first copy).

sections.title: SSD and NVMe
sections.body:
Flash memory has no moving parts, so random access is fast — tens of microseconds — and the seek problem disappears, along with the point of elevator scheduling. But flash has its own quirks. A page can be written only once after its block has been erased, and erasure works on large blocks (hundreds of KB); cells also wear out after a limited number of erase cycles. The SSD controller hides this with a flash translation layer: it writes new data to fresh pages, keeps a map from logical to physical pages, performs wear levelling to spread erases evenly, and runs garbage collection in the background. The OS helps by sending TRIM commands that tell the drive which blocks are free.

NVMe attaches flash directly over the PCIe bus with up to 64 K parallel command queues, removing the old SATA bottleneck and bringing millions of operations per second. Cost per bit remains HDD cheapest, SSD middle, DRAM dearest, which is why systems use all three in a hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Why do elevator algorithms matter little on an SSD?

choices.text: There is no arm to move, so request order barely changes latency.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: NVMe queues deeply.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Seek time was the thing being optimised.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: They have a sophisticated one.

choices.text: Spreading writes and erases evenly over all flash blocks so none wears out early.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The controller remaps hot logical blocks to different physical blocks over time.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It concerns write cycles, not temperature.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It is not a file-system operation.

problems.prompt: Give two reasons why the same file system and scheduler tuned for a hard disk may be a poor fit for an SSD.
problems.answer: (1) HDD schedulers minimise seeks; an SSD has none, so reordering buys little and costs CPU. (2) Defragmenting an HDD to make files contiguous is useless on an SSD and only wastes erase cycles. Also write amplification and wear mean the file system should avoid needless rewrites and issue TRIM.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Controllers have registers; I/O is port- or memory-mapped. Data moves by polling, interrupts or DMA — DMA gives one interrupt per block.
  • The stack: interrupt handler → driver → device-independent layer (buffering, caching, spooling) → user library.
  • Disk access = seek + rotational latency (half a turn) + transfer; random access ≈ 13 ms, so ~76 IOPS.
  • Scheduling: FCFS fair but slow; SSTF fast but may starve; SCAN/LOOK bounded; C-SCAN/C-LOOK uniform.
  • RAID 0 stripes, 1 mirrors, 5 uses XOR parity (capacity (n−1)/n), 6 survives two failures.
  • Stable storage = two copies written in sequence; SSDs trade seek time for erase-block and wear management.
